dailyRead: Start with what is not happening, because it is the most reliable fact in this file. At 05:00 UTC every dollar major is inside a tenth of a percent on the day - EUR/USD 1.11440 and minus 0.09%, GBP/USD 1.33201 and minus 0.05%, USD/JPY 157.806 and minus 0.02%, AUD/USD 0.70529 and minus 0.01%, NZD/USD 0.56205 and minus 0.08%, USD/CAD 1.39841 and minus 0.08%, USD/CHF 0.82852 and plus 0.06%, DXY 102.184 and plus 0.05%. That is not calm, it is a board that has refused to take a position before three central-bank events inside twenty-two hours, and it means the levels quoted in this file are pre-event levels with a short shelf life. The week's information is all in front of us: US advance Q3 GDP at 3.2% forecast against 1.5% previously and September core PCE at 0.3% m/m against 0.2%, both at 12:30 UTC today; the ECB at 13:15 with Lagarde at 13:45; the Bank of Japan statement and Quarterly Outlook Report at 02:30 UTC tomorrow with Ueda at 05:30. Trade the hush accordingly - size for the gap, not for the range. The first real change since yesterday is that the December Fed question has been settled as a pricing matter and reopened as a data matter. The Federal Reserve held the target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent on October 28, and the primary source confirms what this file reported at the time: the statement was approved by a 10-2 vote, with Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack voting against because they preferred to raise the target range by a quarter point at this meeting. Hammack dissented the same way in July; for Cook it is the first dissent of her four years in the post, which is the part that carries information. The statement says inflation remains elevated, that the Committee will deliver price stability, and that job gains have kept pace with the workforce while the unemployment rate has changed little - and, worth noting against yesterday's read, it does not mention energy prices at all, so the energy channel came from Warsh at the podium rather than from the Committee's text. What this file could not see yesterday was the repricing, because it had not printed when the commentary pass ran. It has now: CME FedWatch has December 9 at about 81.4% against 75.1% the previous morning, Polymarket at 82% against roughly 77% pre-decision, and Bloomberg headlining bond traders at 90%; Oxford Economics reads the two hike dissents, the statement wording and officials' prior comments as pointing to a December move. Put that against the labour market the same statement describes as little changed - September non-farm payrolls of plus 29,000 from plus 133,000, unemployment up to 4.2%, consumer confidence at 48.0 and within four points of the series low - and the dollar's problem is unchanged but sharper. There is essentially nothing hawkish left to buy at 81-85%, and the labour market is the leg that breaks first. So today's two prints are the whole trade: a 3.2% GDP beat with core PCE at or above 0.3% is largely paid for, while a miss on either has no forward guidance underneath it to arrest the fall, because Warsh has opposed guidance since his August Jackson Hole speech. The dollar stays at zero and stays MIXED, and the honest instruction is that it has to be bought on prints now, not on words. The second change, and the one that moves the trade list, is sterling. Yesterday this file called Chancellor Healey's first Budget the nearest risk in the book and said the asymmetry sat on the downside. It passed without incident, and that matters more than the Budget's contents. Ten-year gilt yields fell 2.1 basis points to 5.321% on Tradeweb and the thirty-year fell 4.5 basis points to around 5.70%, the FTSE All-Share was flat and sterling was largely unmoved against the dollar; the OBR put fiscal headroom at 15 billion pounds for 2029-30 against 24 billion forecast in March, which is at the low end of the pre-Budget cluster but inside it, and the fiscal rules were kept. Commentators settled on credible, uneventful, boring. A tail risk that does not happen is a repricing, and here is what it clears the way for. The Bank of England held at 3.75% on September 17 on a 6-3 vote with all three dissenters voting for 25 basis points, Governor Bailey said the longer this volatility persists the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate, September CPI then came in at 3.5% against a 3.4% forecast and 3.1% previously with core up to 2.8% from 2.6%, and LSEG pricing has been 98% for a hike to 4.00% on November 5. Behind the policy case the activity mix is quietly the best in the G10 outside the United States: all three PMIs expanding and rising, composite 53.1, services 53.1, manufacturing 52.8; unemployment falling to 4.7% from 4.9% with employment plus 102,000; and the ten-year gilt at 5.3252 is the highest yield on this board. Sterling goes from plus 1 to plus 2 and from MIXED to STRENGTHENING. Be precise about what is and is not new, because the November 5 hike itself is spent at 98%. What is new is that the fiscal tail is gone, that December is only partly priced, and that the market has not paid for any of it in spot - GBP/USD is minus 0.60% on the week and minus 1.04% year to date. That combination, a strong fundamental case with no price performance, is where the edge usually is, and it argues for expressing the pound on crosses rather than against a dollar that has its own two prints today. EUR/GBP short at 0.83663 is the cleanest version: both central banks sit inside a week, one is 98% priced to hike and the other is 70 of 73 economists expecting a hold. The invalidation is specific and worth watching - consumer confidence collapsed to minus 24 from minus 13, wage growth decelerated to 3.7% from 3.9%, and retail sales fell 0.4% m/m, so this is a pound being tightened into a consumer that is already flinching. Third, the oil premium is deflating for the first time in a week, and this time the reason is diplomatic rather than physical. WTI is 101.276 and minus 1.46%, Brent 114.031 and minus 1.12%, and the weekly gain has halved to plus 1.82% from the plus 4.40% this file quoted yesterday; crude is still plus 12.01% on the month. The catalyst is dated: reporting on October 28 has Iran saying the strait could reopen within four to five days if the United States lifts its blockade. That is the invalidation yesterday's USOIL note named in advance, so this file owes a position on it rather than a restatement. The position is that the thesis survives and the asymmetry does not. An Iranian offer conditional on a US concession is not a reopening, and the harder facts all postdate the escalation: the IRGC declared the strait closed on October 26, the International Maritime Organization said on October 27 that the Hormuz route contains mines and that it cannot guarantee safe transit, more than thirty very large crude carriers have been damaged with eleven hit in October alone on a Reuters review of IMO and MarineTraffic data, and war-risk cover is quoted at 6-10% of hull value per transit against 0.15-0.25% before the war. Transits fell from 85 a day to four by October 18 and the barrels that still move do so at night in a US-protected lane. Priced off insurable risk, that premium is intact; what has changed is that there is now a credible path to its removal, with CENTCOM disputing the closure and the UN pushing for talks. USOIL stays LONG but the conviction comes down from MEDIUM to LOW-MED, and the thing that would flip it is an accepted deal rather than another soft session. Canada keeps the benefit either way and keeps plus 2. The Bank of Canada raised the overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.50% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, and the Monetary Policy Report rather than the decision carried the content: the 2027 inflation forecast went to 3.1% from the 2.0% projected in July and 2026 growth to 1.0% from 0.7%, with Macklem saying the hike was needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill into the rest of the economy, that there is no predetermined path, and that further increases would proceed carefully one meeting at a time. The loonie is quietly the second-best major on the month, USD/CAD minus 1.74%, and TradingEconomics now carries the policy rate at 2.50%. The reason this is plus 2 and not plus 3 is the domestic data underneath it, which is the worst on the board: unemployment 6.5% and rising, September employment minus 68,300 after minus 41,700 in August, the composite PMI at 48.7 in contraction, business confidence down to 58.2 from 64.3, and core CPI at 2.2% and falling. This is a central bank tightening on an import price it does not control, into a labour market that is shedding jobs, with December only about 42% priced. Own it against the franc and the kiwi, where the gap is three points, rather than reaching for more against the dollar. Australia keeps the top of the board at plus 3 and the story is now entirely about where you express it. The policy rate is 4.60%, the highest here; headline CPI is 4.3% y/y and accelerating; TradingEconomics carries the core measure at 3.6% y/y against 3.5% previously, while wire reports put the quarterly trimmed mean's annual rate at 3.7% against a 3.6% consensus - a discrepancy worth naming rather than smoothing, and TE is the number this file uses. Cash-rate futures have moved to about 85% for a hike to 4.85% on November 3 from 60-69% before the CPI, ANZ and Westpac call the hike and NAB has joined them, with CBA still at a pause. AUD/USD is plus 0.46% on the week, plus 1.52% on the month and plus 5.70% year to date, the best major of the year. The counterweight has not improved and is the reason the expression matters: the services PMI is 47.8 and the composite 47.7, both in contraction, unemployment is at a five-year-high 4.7%, September employment fell 39,329 and consumer confidence dropped to 80.4 from 84.4. A hike priced at 85% into a contracting service sector is not something to buy against the dollar; it is something to own against the kiwi and the franc, where the score gap is four points. AUD/NZD at 1.25485 stays the single highest-conviction trade in the file, and the reason is that it passed its test. New Zealand stays at minus 1 and WEAKENING, and the point is the absence of a bounce: NZD/USD is 0.56205, still minus 1.08% on the week, having recovered only a quarter of a percent from the post-decision low in the twenty-eight hours since the Reserve Bank held at 2.75% on a 4-3 vote against pricing near 90% for a hike. Yesterday this file corrected itself for reading Breman's hawkish conditional guidance as a floor; the price has now confirmed that correction twice over. Be fair to the other side, though, because it is not a one-way score. New Zealand's survey data is the strongest on this board - the manufacturing PMI is 56.5, the composite 53.4 and rising, business confidence 52.5 and consumer confidence jumped to 89.5 from 80.4 - and inflation is actually falling, 3.7% from 4.1%, which is the respectable case for the hold the Committee delivered. December 9 carries a full Monetary Policy Statement and TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00%, so a 4-3 vote means one member switching reverses this, with the November 7 election in between. Short the kiwi against the Aussie and the loonie, not into December blind. The yen is the biggest binary and the most honest MIXED on the board. USD/JPY at 157.806 is 0.28% stronger for the yen than the 158.250 this file quoted after the Fed, which is a small firming into the event rather than a trend. The Bank of Japan meets at 02:30 UTC tomorrow and is expected to hold at 1.25%: more than 80% of economists in a Bloomberg survey see the next hike in December and none see one in October, and the live question is the Quarterly Outlook Report at 02:31, which sources say may lift the inflation forecast for the next fiscal year because higher oil prices are pressing on prices for longer than expected. The case for the yen is that core CPI has jumped to 2.1% from 1.7%, headline is 2.1%, and the JGB ten-year is 2.8280; the case against is a US-Japan ten-year spread still at 217 basis points, wage growth decelerating to 3.8% from 4.3%, and an economy importing a barrel that is up 12% on the month. A hawkish Outlook Report that raises next year's inflation forecast is the cleanest yen-positive outcome available this week, and a guarded Ueda at 05:30 is the opposite. Zero, MIXED, and JPYBASKET stays RANGE by the rule - but every XXX/JPY position in this file is a view on tomorrow morning whether you intend it or not. Europe is the one place where the two indices have genuinely separated, and it is worth scoring on its own evidence. The DAX is 25,761.10 and plus 0.44% today, up 2.23% on the month and 6.81% on the year. The Euro Stoxx 50 is 6,174.90 and plus 0.03%, down 1.50% on the month against the DAX's plus 2.23% - a 3.7-point divergence inside four weeks - and the reason is the bank weight that usually carries it: Euro Stoxx Banks is 281.27, minus 0.56% on the day and minus 10.50% on the month, even with a December ECB hike that 64 of 73 economists expect. When the heaviest sector falls 10% into a tightening that should help it, something else is dominating, and the candidate is French: the CAC is minus 1.85% on the month and minus 3.83% on the year, and the OAT-Bund spread at 155.9 basis points is repaired but not healed. The euro itself stays at zero. HICP at 3.8% is a three-year high and core is 2.5% and rising, which is why 64 of 73 economists expect 25 basis points in December and OIS prices about 70 basis points of hikes over twelve months; against that, every activity series has turned - the composite PMI down to 51.9 from 53.1, services 51.7 from 53.0, manufacturing 52.4 from 52.9, consumer confidence minus 17.9, wage growth down to 3.0% from 3.4% - and EUR/USD is minus 5.08% year to date, the worst major of 2026. The ECB holds today with about a 3% chance of a move priced, so the only thing that trades is Lagarde at 13:45 and how explicitly she points at December. The franc stays at the bottom with the kiwi, and the reason is now policy rather than flows. The SNB policy rate is 0.00% against inflation of 1.0%, the Swiss ten-year is 0.4990 - the lowest here by 237 basis points - and Bloomberg reported on October 22 that the Bank judged its threat of franc sales no longer necessary at the September 24 meeting because war-induced haven flows into the currency had subsided. The franc is the weakest major on the week, USD/CHF plus 0.99%, which is exactly what a zero-rate funding currency does when the haven bid leaves. The asymmetry to respect is that EUR/CHF at 0.9233 is back near the level at which the SNB previously threatened to step up intervention, which puts a soft floor under the cross and a cap on franc strength; and a genuine Hormuz re-escalation re-bids the franc faster than any of this. Short it where the gap is widest - against the Aussie, the pound and the loonie, all three points or more. Finally the metals, where the interesting thing is a split rather than a level. Gold is 4042.87 and minus 0.61%, up 0.45% on the week and down 2.76% on the month, still holding the 4,000 handle dealers treat as support, and its two legs are pulling against each other: a US ten-year at 5.0020 and a December hike at 81-85% are real-rate negative, while Hormuz is haven-positive. Silver is 53.361 and minus 1.09%, minus 2.25% on the week and minus 11.66% on the month, so the gold-silver ratio has widened to about 75.8. Copper, meanwhile, is 6.6305 dollars a pound and plus 4.21% on the week. That is the split worth trading: copper is being paid for its industrial leg - the Codelco El Teniente mudslide, Fastmarkets estimating 200,000 to 400,000 tonnes of incremental AI data-centre demand in 2026, tariff-driven stockpiling - and silver is not being paid for the same leg at all, which makes short silver against long copper the cleanest relative expression in the commodity block and keeps copper aligned with the Australian long. Risk appetite itself is unbothered: the S&P is 7,726.14 and plus 0.28%, the Nasdaq 100 29,485.64 and plus 0.55%, and the VIX is down to 16.91. Equities firm with a US ten-year at 5% is still the inflation-premium configuration rather than the growth-scare one, and that is the backdrop every trade in this file sits on.

today.headline: Lagarde took back most of what the statement withheld - the hold was unanimous, the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate, and the direction of travel is quite clear on rates - and the euro recovered a fresh 17-month low at 1.1105 to trade 1.11503 and minus 0.03%
today.read: This is the rare press conference that reversed the text it was meant to explain, and the tape is the proof: the statement at 13:15 took EUR/USD from minus 0.09% to minus 0.29% and down to a 17-month low at 1.1105, and the hour with Lagarde brought it back to 1.11503 and minus 0.03%. Three things did that work. The hold was decided unanimously, but she volunteered that the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate - that is a Council arguing about tightening, not about waiting. She said the direction of travel is quite clear on rates, which is the closest this Council comes to naming a destination while refusing to pre-commit to the path. And she framed the inter-meeting window as information rather than delay, saying six more weeks will give the Council a lot more, while adding that there is no plan to restrict the number of meetings. Set against that is a genuine dovish brake, and it is hers too: there is no risk of second-round effects beyond what is in the projections, indirect effects from energy have increased but wage pressures remain moderate, compensation per employee slowed to 3.3% in Q2 from 3.6% in Q1, and the ECB wage tracker points to 2.5-2.8% for the rest of 2026 and an average 2.6% through the first three quarters of 2027 - below what a 3.8% headline would normally force. That is why the euro stays at zero and MIXED rather than moving: the hike is live, the second-round mechanism that would make it urgent is not, and the headline is an energy pass-through that monetary policy cannot shorten. Forward, December 17 is the trade and the evidence arrives before it - German preliminary CPI at 07:29 and GDP at 09:00 UTC tomorrow, then euro-area flash HICP, with the wage tracker the series that decides whether the Council gets to keep waiting. The French question is the other half and it did not improve: the ten-year OAT is 4.910% near quarter-century highs, the OAT-Bund spread is wider at about 158 basis points against 155.9 this morning, and Lagarde stayed cool on the Transmission Protection Instrument, offering only that if market developments threatened transmission the ECB has instruments to respond. Her exit on 7 February 2027 leaves her chairing two more decisions, 17 December and 4 February, which is one more reason the destination is stated and the path is not.

today.headline: Advance Q3 GDP printed 3.4% annualised against a 3.2% forecast - the fastest in a year, up from 2.2% - while September core PCE came in line at 0.3% m/m with August revised up from 0.2% to 0.3%, the annual core rate to 3.1% from 3.0% and headline PCE to 3.6% from 3.4%; initial claims beat at 194K against 199K, and DXY answered all of it with 102.209 and plus 0.01%
today.read: The asymmetry this file described has resolved on the side it called already paid for, and the price is the proof: a one-year-high growth print, a rising annual core PCE and claims below consensus bought the dollar essentially nothing. That is what spent means, so the dollar moves to plus 1 on the data without becoming a buy against the board - the score rises because the growth leg of the macro block genuinely firmed, not because there is a rally to chase. Hold on to the one disinflationary line, because it is inside the same report: Q3 core PCE prices slowed to 2.5% annualised from 3.3%, which is the thread DBS was pulling pre-release when it argued resilient growth with easing underlying inflation should make markets question the 2027 hikes they have priced. Forward, December 9 is no longer the question. The questions are the October payroll report, where plus 29,000 and a 4.2% unemployment rate leave the dollar its only soft leg, and the November 3 midterms - and with Warsh still refusing forward guidance, a labour miss has nothing underneath it to arrest the fall. That remains the one real tail.

snapshot.t: The Budget passed without a gilt shock, and that cleared tail is why the pound goes to plus 2
snapshot.s: Ten-year gilts fell 2.1 basis points to 5.321% and the thirty-year 4.5 basis points to around 5.70%; sterling was largely unmoved and the FTSE All-Share flat. The OBR put headroom at 15 billion pounds for 2029-30 against 24 billion in March, at the low end of the pre-Budget cluster but inside it, with the fiscal rules kept. That clears the runway for November 5, 98% priced on LSEG data for a hike to 4.00% after September's 6-3 vote with three members already voting for it - behind the best PMI mix in the G10 ex-US and the highest yield on this board at 5.3252. The pound has not been paid for any of it: minus 0.60% on the week.

snapshot.t: The crude premium eases for the first time in a week on Iran's conditional offer to reopen Hormuz
snapshot.s: WTI is 101.276 and minus 1.46%, Brent 114.031 and minus 1.12%, and the weekly gain has halved to plus 1.82% from plus 4.40% yesterday, though crude is still plus 12.01% on the month. The harder facts are intact: the IMO said on October 27 the route contains mines and it cannot guarantee safe transit, more than thirty VLCCs are damaged with eleven in October, and war-risk cover runs 6-10% of hull value against 0.15-0.25% pre-war. snapshot.t: Lagarde turned her own statement around at the podium - unanimous hold, but the Council debated a hike
snapshot.s: The text at 13:15 withheld December; the press conference at 13:45 handed most of it back. Lagarde said the decision to hold was unanimous, that the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate, that the direction of travel is quite clear on rates, and that six more weeks will give the Council a lot more information - against her own dovish brake, that there is no risk of second-round effects beyond what is in the projections and that the ECB wage tracker points to 2.5-2.8% for the rest of 2026 and an average 2.6% through the first three quarters of 2027. EUR/USD printed a fresh 17-month low at 1.1105 on the statement and has recovered to 1.11503 and minus 0.03%; sterling still holds a 17-month high against it at 0.83533. Europe read it as rate relief for duration and a problem for banks: the DAX is 26,100.90 and plus 1.54%, a two-month high and a fourth straight advance, while Euro Stoxx Banks is 278.95 and minus 0.82%, minus 10.23% on the month, with the French ten-year at 4.910% near quarter-century highs and the OAT-Bund spread wider at about 158 basis points. Lagarde stayed cool on the Transmission Protection Instrument, saying only that if market developments threatened transmission the ECB has instruments to respond.

EUR.note: Held on October 29 - deposit 2.50%, main refinancing 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90% - and the press conference is what set the path. Lagarde said the hold was decided unanimously, that the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate, that the direction of travel is quite clear on rates, and that the inter-meeting period gives the Council a lot more information; she also said there is no plan to restrict the number of meetings. December therefore stays the base case, consistent with 64 of 73 economists expecting 25 basis points and futures pricing read above 80% into this meeting. The brake is the wage evidence she cited herself: compensation per employee grew 3.3% in Q2 from 3.6% in Q1, the ECB wage tracker points to 2.5-2.8% for the remaining months of 2026 and an average 2.6% for the first three quarters of 2027, and she said there is no risk of second-round effects beyond what is in the projections. The November 5 hike itself is spent; what is owned here is the cleared fiscal tail and a live December.

symbols.why: Stays SHORT at 1.55978 on a zero-against-plus-two gap, and the press conference did not change the ranking: the euro has a probable December hike it has talked itself into, while Canada has a delivered one - 2.50% on October 28, the first since July 2023, with the 2027 inflation forecast lifted to 3.1% from 2.0%. Lagarde restored December without pre-committing and simultaneously named the brake, no second-round effects beyond the projections and a wage tracker at 2.6% for 2027, so the euro leg is firmer than the statement left it but no more than that.
symbols.risk: The energy leg has turned further against the Canadian side since the decision: WTI is 100.501 and minus 2.22%, Brent 113.655 and minus 1.44%, so Iran’s conditional Hormuz offer keeps cutting the terms-of-trade windfall the hike was insurance against, while cheaper crude and EU gas at minus 3.30% are a straight tailwind for a euro area that imports all of it. That remains the real risk here rather than either central bank. Canada’s labour market is the other half - 6.5% unemployment, employment minus 68,300, December only about 42% priced - and Canadian monthly GDP lands at 12:30 UTC tomorrow.

symbols.why: Stays LONG at 0.92222, a touch lower than the 0.9233 quoted before the ECB and therefore a touch closer to the zone where the SNB previously threatened to step up intervention - which is still the asymmetry holding this up rather than any euro strength. The press conference helped the euro leg at the margin, with Lagarde restoring the December hike the statement had withheld, but a Council that says the direction of travel is clear while refusing to pre-commit is not a catalyst for a narrow cross. The franc side is a 0.00% rate against 1.0% inflation with the haven bid still ebbing - gold minus 0.87%, silver minus 2.34%, WTI minus 2.22%.

The structural risk is Hormuz: a genuine re-escalation re-bids the franc faster than anything in this file and takes this straight into the SNB’s zone, the mirror image of why today’s easing crude helps. The newer risk is European rather than Swiss - a French financing accident, with the OAT at 4.910% and the spread wider at about 158 basis points, pushes haven flows into exactly this cross.

symbols.why: Upgraded to LONG at 210.20 on the pound going to plus 2 against a zero yen. The sterling case is a 98%-priced hike to 4.00% on November 5 with the Budget tail cleared, the highest yield on this board at 5.3252, all three PMIs expanding and unemployment falling to 4.7%. The yen holds at 1.25% with a 2.8280 JGB and wage growth decelerating to 3.8% from 4.3%.
symbols.risk: The whole position is a view on the Bank of Japan tomorrow morning whether you intend it or not. The 02:31 UTC Quarterly Outlook Report is the live item - sources say it may lift next fiscal year's inflation forecast on oil, which pre-commits December and would hit this cross hard given its beta to yen strength. Tokyo core CPI at 23:30 UTC tonight is the first input. On the pound side the invalidation is the consumer: confidence at minus 24 from minus 13 and retail sales minus 0.4% m/m. This is the highest-beta pound long in the file.

symbols.why: Stays SHORT at 1.88860 but the conviction comes down, because the pound upgrade to plus 2 narrows this to a one-point gap from two. The Aussie still has the better absolute case - a 4.60% policy rate against 3.75%, CPI accelerating to 4.3% against 3.5%, and plus 5.70% year to date - but both currencies are now near-certain to hike inside eight days, at 85% for November 3 and 98% for November 5.
symbols.risk: The narrowest score gap of any directional trade in this file and the reason it is LOW-MED. Both hikes are priced, so this turns on the activity comparison, and that comparison has actually moved toward the pound: UK PMIs are 53.1, 53.1 and 52.8 and all rising while Australia's services PMI is 47.8 and composite 47.7 and both contracting, with UK unemployment falling to 4.7% as Australia's rises to the same level. A soft Australian employment print before November 3 would flip this outright.

symbols.why: Upgraded in conviction at 2.36991 on the pound going to plus 2 against a minus-one kiwi, a three-point gap. One central bank is 98% priced to hike on November 5 with its fiscal tail just cleared; the other refused a hike priced near 90% on a 4-3 vote and has seen its currency recover only a quarter of a percent in twenty-eight hours. The yield gap is 5.3252 against 4.8850 and widening.
symbols.risk: The kiwi side is the live half and it is not one-way: New Zealand's manufacturing PMI at 56.5 and composite at 53.4 are the strongest survey set here, consumer confidence jumped to 89.5 from 80.4, inflation is falling to 3.7% from 4.1%, and December 9 carries a full Monetary Policy Statement with TE forecasting 3.00% - one member switching from 4-3 reverses it, with the November 7 election in between. On the pound side, consumer confidence at minus 24 from minus 13 is the warning underneath the tightening.

symbols.why: Moves from a view to RANGE at 1.86270, because the pound's upgrade to plus 2 has made this two equal scores. Both currencies are tightening into weak domestic demand and both have a live near-term decision: the Bank of England at 98% for November 5, the Bank of Canada having already delivered 2.50% with December about 42% priced. With the scores level the trade is levels rather than direction.
symbols.risk: The legs separate on energy, which is the thing to watch for a directional case later. Canada gains from a crude premium the Bank explicitly hiked to insure against, so Iran's conditional offer to reopen Hormuz cuts the Canadian side - WTI is already minus 1.46% - while cheaper energy helps a UK CPI that just printed 3.5% on energy pass-through. The labour comparison points the other way: UK unemployment falling to 4.7% with employment plus 102,000 against Canada at 6.5% and minus 68,300.

symbols.why: Upgraded to LONG at 1.10360 on a three-point gap, plus 2 against minus 1, and it is the cleanest pound expression after EUR/GBP because the franc leg has no event risk this week. Sterling is 98% priced to hike to 4.00% on November 5 with its Budget tail cleared and carries the highest yield here at 5.3252; the franc is a 0.00% rate against 1.0% inflation with the lowest ten-year at 0.4990, a 483 basis point gap.
symbols.risk: The franc is a haven and this is therefore a short-volatility position dressed as a carry trade. A genuine Hormuz re-escalation re-bids the franc faster than anything else in the file and would cut this hard, which is exactly why today's conditional reopening offer is the trade's friend. The SNB's intervention zone is a secondary comfort - it caps franc strength rather than guaranteeing weakness. On the pound side, consumer confidence at minus 24 from minus 13 and wages decelerating to 3.7% are the invalidation.

symbols.why: Stays LONG at 111.30 on a plus-three-against-zero gap, the widest the Aussie has against any zero-scored currency. The rate differential is 4.60% against 1.25% with the Australian ten-year at 5.1800 against a 2.8280 JGB, and the risk backdrop supports it: the S&P is plus 0.28%, the Nasdaq 100 plus 0.55% and the VIX down to 16.91.
symbols.risk: A high-beta carry pair into the week's biggest binary. The 02:31 UTC Quarterly Outlook Report is the risk - a lifted inflation forecast for next fiscal year pre-commits a December hike and this is the kind of cross that gaps on it - with Tokyo core CPI at 23:30 UTC tonight as the first tell. The Australian half is also less one-way than the score suggests: the November 3 hike is 85% priced, so the asymmetry is spent, and a contracting services PMI at 47.8 with employment minus 39,329 is the domestic warning.

symbols.why: Stays the highest-conviction trade in the file at 1.25485, a four-point score gap and the widest on the board, and it has now passed its test twice. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand refused a hike priced near 90% on a 4-3 vote twenty-eight hours ago and the kiwi has recovered only a quarter of a percent; the Reserve Bank of Australia is about 85% priced to hike to 4.85% on November 3 on a verified core beat. Policy rates 4.60% against 2.75%, inflation accelerating to 4.3% against falling to 3.7%.
symbols.risk: Both meetings land inside six weeks and the kiwi side is the one that can reverse. December 9 carries a full Monetary Policy Statement and the first new OCR track since September, and a 4-3 vote means a single member switching delivers the hike this trade is short - with the November 7 New Zealand election in between and the strongest survey data on this board underneath, including a 56.5 manufacturing PMI and consumer confidence jumping to 89.5 from 80.4. On the Australian side a soft employment print before November 3 cuts the hike and this cross together.

symbols.why: Stays LONG at 0.98628 but this is the narrowest Aussie long in the file, a one-point gap between plus 3 and plus 2. The Australian case is the higher rate at 4.60% against 2.50% and accelerating inflation at 4.3% against 3.1%; the Canadian case is a hike already delivered and a terms-of-trade leg still intact with WTI plus 12.01% on the month.
symbols.risk: Both are commodity currencies with central banks in a tightening posture, so the trade is thin by construction. The honest risk is that Canada's leg is improving while Australia's is priced: the Bank of Canada has delivered and lifted its 2027 inflation forecast to 3.1% from 2.0%, while the November 3 RBA hike is already 85% paid. Against that, Canada's labour market is the worst here at 6.5% unemployment and minus 68,300 jobs, and Iran's conditional reopening offer cuts the barrel the loonie leans on. Keep this small or express the Aussie against the kiwi and the franc instead.

symbols.why: Stays HIGH at 0.58435 on a four-point gap, tied with AUD/NZD for the widest on the board, and the carry is the most extreme pairing available here: a 4.60% policy rate against 0.00%, and an Australian ten-year at 5.1800 against a Swiss 0.4990 for a 468 basis point spread. The franc has no event risk this week and the SNB dropped its intervention threat on September 24 as haven flows ebbed, while risk appetite is firm with the VIX at 16.91.
symbols.risk: This is leveraged long risk and long the Hormuz premium deflating, so name the tail plainly: a genuine re-escalation re-bids the franc and sells the Aussie simultaneously, which is the one configuration that hits both legs at once. Today's conditional reopening offer is why the trade works now, and an accepted deal would extend it. The Australian half carries its own warning - an 85%-priced hike, a contracting services PMI at 47.8 and employment minus 39,329 - and the SNB's intervention zone caps franc strength rather than guaranteeing weakness.

symbols.why: Stays SHORT at 88.69 on a minus-one-against-zero gap. The kiwi leg is the one with the fresh evidence: a 4-3 vote refused a hike priced near 90% and the currency has recovered only a quarter of a percent in twenty-eight hours, still minus 1.08% on the week. The yen holds at 1.25% with core CPI jumping to 2.1% from 1.7%.
symbols.risk: Two currencies with live central-bank reversal risk on opposite sides, which is why this is LOW-MED. The yen leg is the near one: a guarded Ueda at 05:30 UTC with the US spread still at 217 basis points sells the yen and cuts this short, while a hawkish Outlook Report at 02:31 extends it. The kiwi leg is the slower one: the strongest survey data on this board, falling inflation at 3.7% from 4.1%, and a December 9 Monetary Policy Statement where one member switching from 4-3 delivers the hike. Prefer AUD/NZD for the kiwi short.

symbols.why: Stays SHORT at 0.78598 on a three-point gap, minus 1 against plus 2, and it is the cleanest kiwi short after AUD/NZD because both central banks met on the same day and went opposite ways. The Bank of Canada raised to 2.50% and lifted its 2027 inflation forecast to 3.1% from 2.0%; the Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% against pricing near 90% for a hike on a 4-3 vote.
symbols.risk: The Canadian leg's rationale is energy, and that is what Iran's conditional offer to reopen Hormuz undercuts - WTI at minus 1.46% is the first move in that direction, and the hike was explicitly insurance against the premium. Canada's labour market is the worst on this board at 6.5% unemployment and employment minus 68,300, with December only about 42% priced. On the kiwi side, December 9 brings a full Monetary Policy Statement and TE forecasts 3.00%, so one switcher from 4-3 reverses this. Canadian monthly GDP at 12:30 UTC tomorrow.

symbols.why: Stays RANGE at 0.46567 and it is the one pair in this file where both legs score minus 1, so there is no directional case to make. The kiwi is weak because a 4-3 vote refused a paid-for hike; the franc is weak because a 0.00% rate without a haven bid is a funding currency. Two weakening currencies paired against each other is a levels trade and nothing else.
symbols.risk: The two legs respond to opposite shocks, which is what makes this a genuine range rather than a coincidence. A Hormuz re-escalation bids the franc and sells the kiwi, taking this sharply lower; an accepted reopening deal does the reverse. The scheduled risk is all on the kiwi side - December 9 with a full Monetary Policy Statement where one member switching from 4-3 delivers a hike, and the November 7 election - while the SNB does not meet until December 10. Lowest conviction in the file by design.

symbols.why: Stays LONG at 112.85 on a plus-two-against-zero gap and it remains the trade that keeps the oil view and the currency view consistent. The Bank of Canada delivered 2.50% on October 28 with its 2027 inflation forecast lifted to 3.1% from 2.0%; Japan imports the barrel that Canada sells, and WTI is still plus 12.01% on the month even after today's minus 1.46%.
symbols.risk: Both legs lean on the same crude price in opposite directions, so Hormuz is the single factor that matters most. Iran's conditional offer to reopen the strait cuts the Canadian leg and helps the Japanese one simultaneously - the one shock that hits this cross from both sides - and an accepted deal would be the clean invalidation. The scheduled risk is the BoJ: a hawkish Quarterly Outlook Report at 02:31 UTC that lifts next fiscal year's inflation forecast takes this lower. Canada's labour market at 6.5% unemployment and minus 68,300 jobs is the slower warning.

symbols.why: Stays LONG at 0.59247 on a three-point gap, plus 2 against minus 1, and the franc leg has no event risk this week which makes this a cleaner loonie long than USD/CAD. Canada has a delivered hike to 2.50%, a 2027 inflation forecast lifted to 3.1% from 2.0% and a 3.8580 ten-year; Switzerland has a 0.00% rate against 1.0% inflation and the lowest yield on this board at 0.4990.
symbols.risk: Both currencies are energy-levered in opposite directions and both respond to Hormuz, so the tail is shared with CAD/JPY: a genuine re-escalation bids the franc as a haven while an accepted reopening deal removes the premium the Canadian hike was insurance against. Today's conditional offer is mildly negative for the Canadian leg and mildly positive for the trade's franc leg, which roughly offsets. Canada's own invalidation is domestic: 6.5% unemployment, employment minus 68,300 after minus 41,700, a 48.7 composite PMI and December only about 42% priced.

symbols.why: Stays SHORT at 190.47 on a minus-one-against-zero gap. The franc is the weakest major on the week with a 0.00% rate against 1.0% inflation and the SNB having dropped its intervention threat on September 24; the yen at least has core CPI jumping to 2.1% from 1.7%, a 2.8280 JGB and a central bank that has already hiked twice this year.
symbols.risk: A pair of havens traded against each other, which means the usual risk-regime logic does not apply and both legs move on their own central banks. The near risk is the BoJ: a guarded Ueda at 05:30 UTC sells the yen and cuts this short, while a hawkish Outlook Report at 02:31 extends it, with Tokyo core CPI at 23:30 tonight as the first input. The franc leg's risk is Hormuz - a re-escalation bids the franc harder than the yen because the yen is also an energy importer - which is why today's conditional reopening offer supports this short.

symbols.why: Stays RANGE at 102.092 and minus 0.10%, and both of its two heavy catalysts have now fired without resolving it. The dollar leg beat and was not paid - advance Q3 GDP 3.4% against 3.2%, annual core PCE to 3.1%, claims 194K - and the euro leg at 57.6% weight gave the index a brief lift on the statement and handed it straight back when Lagarde said the Council had debated a hike and that the direction of travel is quite clear on rates. An index that cannot rise on its own hawkish data or on a dovish-read ECB statement is telling you the carry is priced on both sides.
symbols.risk: Composition keeps this MEDIUM at best. The yen weight at 13.6% carries the Bank of Japan statement and Quarterly Outlook Report at 02:30-02:31 UTC tomorrow, which is now the largest single input left this week, and the Canadian weight at 9.1% has monthly GDP at 12:30. The dollar’s own next move is the October payroll report rather than anything said, because Warsh has opposed forward guidance since August - and with December at 81-85%, a labour miss has nothing underneath it. The November 3 midterms are the political tail.

symbols.why: Stays RANGE by the rule, because the basket rises when the yen strengthens and the yen is MIXED at zero rather than STRENGTHENING. The yen has firmed 0.28% from the 158.250 quoted after the Fed, which is a drift into the event rather than a trend, and the US-Japan ten-year spread is still 217 basis points with wage growth decelerating to 3.8% from 4.3%.
symbols.risk: This is the single cleanest instrument in the file for tomorrow morning and the opposite ticket to every XXX/JPY line here, so it is where a yen view belongs if you have one. A Quarterly Outlook Report at 02:31 UTC that lifts next fiscal year's inflation forecast on oil pre-commits a December hike and sends this higher; a guarded Ueda at 05:30 with the US spread intact sends it lower. Tokyo core CPI at 23:30 UTC tonight, forecast 2.6% against 2.7%, is the first input and the first chance to size.

symbols.why: Staying LONG and the tell is what happened after Lagarde, not before: the index is 26,100.90 and plus 1.54%, a two-month high and a fourth consecutive advance, and it extended its gains while the podium was putting the December hike back on the table. An index of long-duration industrials that rallies through a hawkish-leaning press conference is being driven by something stronger than the discount rate, and the candidates are visible - crude easing to 100.501 and minus 2.22%, EU gas off 3.30% to 97.03 euros a megawatt hour, and AI-related business investment that the ECB itself named as supporting manufacturing, digital services and exports.
symbols.risk: The offset is the one the ECB put at the centre of its statement: energy prices have continued to rise and the European part of that is gas, not crude - EU gas is still plus 34.10% on the month and German gas plus 44.27% on the year, a direct input cost for exactly this index. So the relief is the conditional leg, resting on a Hormuz deal nobody has accepted, while the squeeze is the structural one. Conviction stays MEDIUM rather than rising on a two-month high: German preliminary CPI at 07:29 and Q3 GDP at 09:00 UTC tomorrow are the domestic inputs, with GDP forecast at just 0.1% q/q, and a firmer December hike is a headwind this index has not yet been asked to pay for.

symbols.why: Stays RANGE at 6,211.90 and plus 0.74%, and the press conference sharpened the reason this is scored apart from the DAX rather than softening it. Same session, same ECB: the DAX is plus 1.54% and this is plus 0.74%, because Euro Stoxx Banks - the heaviest sector here and absent there - is 278.95 and minus 0.82% on the day, minus 10.23% on the month. The bank weight was offered a firmer December hike from the podium and still sold, which points at the other leg: the French ten-year is 4.910% near quarter-century highs, the OAT-Bund spread is wider at about 158 basis points against 155.9 this morning, and Lagarde stayed cool on the Transmission Protection Instrument, offering only that if market developments threatened transmission the ECB has instruments to respond.
symbols.risk: That is what RANGE means here: easing crude and AI investment lift the industrial weight it shares with the DAX, while sovereign-spread risk sits on the bank weight the DAX does not carry, and today both pulled at once. The French leg is now the dominant one and it is the thing to watch rather than the ECB - a credible fiscal or TPI resolution re-rates the banks before the industrials, and a further OAT widening does the reverse regardless of what happens to the index’s exporters. FR40 at plus 1.24% and IT40 at plus 0.52% against a DAX at plus 1.54% is the same ranking in miniature.

symbols.why: Stays RANGE at 4026.25 and minus 1.02%, still above the 4,000 handle dealers treat as support but with the upside leg of its axis now spent. The arbiter this file named was September core PCE, and it printed in line at 0.3% m/m with the annual rate up to 3.1% and headline PCE at 3.6%, alongside a 3.4% GDP beat and claims at 194K - no soft print, so no real-rate relief, and gold is the weakest haven on the session. What keeps this a range rather than a short is the Hormuz floor underneath it.
symbols.risk: The tilt inside the range is now lower and 4,000 is the trigger: losing that handle turns this into a short, holding it keeps the two legs balanced. The haven leg is two-sided and that is the whole argument - Iran's conditional offer to reopen the strait sells gold alongside crude, while the IMO's October 27 statement that the route contains mines keeps a floor under it. Against that, a US ten-year at 5.0020 and a December hike at 81-85% are straight real-rate negatives that today's growth print reinforced. The next scheduled real-rate input is the October payroll report, not a Fed speech.

symbols.why: Stays SHORT at 52.492, minus 2.70% on the day and minus 3.84% on the week, and the conviction goes up from LOW-MED because the named reversal catalyst failed to arrive. A soft core PCE was the print that would have lifted both metals; instead it came in line at 0.3% m/m with its annual rate rising to 3.1% against a 3.4% GDP beat, so the real-rate leg stays against silver. The industrial leg is not paying either - copper is plus 3.22% on the week on genuine supply news while silver is down on the day, the week and the month - and the gold-silver ratio has widened further to about 76.7.
symbols.risk: Silver is the most volatile instrument in this file and shorts in it get punished fast, which is why this is MEDIUM rather than higher even with the catalyst resolved. The reversal is a Hormuz re-escalation that re-bids precious metals as a complex, where silver outruns gold on the way up as reliably as it has underperformed on the way down. Tight physical supply remains the structural argument against the trade, and the next real-rate input that could cut it is the October payroll report.

symbols.why: Stays LONG at 6.5672 dollars a pound, minus 1.19% on the session but plus 3.22% on the week, and today's US growth print supports the leg this trade is actually built on. Advance Q3 GDP beat at 3.4% annualised, and the components the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker expected to drive it were equipment investment up 20.9% and intellectual property up 6.6% - the demand side of the AI build-out that Fastmarkets sizes at 200,000 to 400,000 tonnes of incremental data-centre demand in 2026. Treat that composition as the tracker's rather than confirmed, because the BEA component detail is not yet in TE's table. The supply side is unchanged and dated: the Codelco El Teniente mudslide removed capacity from a market already short of spare, tariff-driven stockpiling is tightening availability, and three-month LME copper set a record near 14,858 dollars a tonne on September 9.
symbols.risk: A rally one broker has already called unsustainable, trading in a tight band near its record for six weeks, which is a setup that resolves sharply - and today's minus 1.19% is the kind of session that comes with it. The China demand leg is the one to watch and the PMIs are the input; a global growth scare would cut this and the Aussie together, which is the correlation to respect rather than diversify into. The paired expression against short silver is still the cleaner way to own the industrial thesis, because it strips out the real-rate leg both metals share.

symbols.why: Stays LONG at 101.981 and minus 0.78%, a second session of the premium coming off, with the demand leg marginally better and the risk leg marginally worse. Advance Q3 GDP at 3.4% annualised, the fastest in a year, is a genuine demand-side positive and the strongest argument this thesis gained today; TE still carries crude plus 2.52% on the week and plus 12.70% on the month, so the monthly premium is intact while the weekly one keeps bleeding. Against that, the invalidation named yesterday is live: reporting on October 28 has Iran saying the strait could reopen in four to five days if the United States lifts its blockade.
symbols.risk: An offer conditional on a US concession is not a reopening, and the harder facts are intact - the IMO said on October 27 that the Hormuz route contains mines and that it cannot guarantee safe transit, more than thirty VLCCs are damaged with eleven hit in October on a Reuters review, and war-risk cover runs 6-10% of hull value per transit against 0.15-0.25% pre-war. The flip is an accepted deal rather than another soft session: transits fell from 85 a day to four by October 18 and the barrels still moving do so at night in a US-protected lane, so the premium is priced off insurable risk rather than volumes. Stays consistent with a plus 2 CAD, a short USD/CAD at cut conviction and a long CAD/JPY, all of which share this invalidation.

catalysts.event: Australia: CPI m/m, CPI y/y and Trimmed Mean CPI m/m (ABS red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Headline CPI printed above forecast at 4.3% y/y and TradingEconomics carries the core measure at 3.6% from 3.5%, while wire reports put the quarterly trimmed mean's annual rate at 3.7% against a 3.6% consensus - a discrepancy named rather than smoothed, with TE the figure this file uses. Cash-rate futures moved to about 85% for a November 3 hike to 4.85% from 60-69% before the release; ANZ and Westpac call the hike and NAB has joined them, with CBA still at a pause.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision and Rate Statement (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. The Bank held the OCR at 2.75% against a 3.00% forecast and pricing near 90%, on a 4-3 vote. This was the dovish surprise of the week and it took the kiwi to minus 1; twenty-eight hours on, NZD/USD has recovered only a quarter of a percent and is still minus 1.08% on the week, which is the confirmation rather than the decision.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ press conference with Governor Breman (red folder)
catalysts.note: Held. Breman said further increases are likely at coming meetings and could take policy into restrictive territory, and that the Committee is concerned a sustained weak New Zealand dollar adds to imported inflation. The price has refused that floor twice now, which is why this file withdrew the argument and keeps the kiwi at minus 1. December 9 carries a full Monetary Policy Statement and TE forecasts 3.00%.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: Annual Budget Release (HM Treasury red folder)
catalysts.note: Delivered, and the tail did not happen - which is itself the repricing. Ten-year gilt yields fell 2.1 basis points to 5.321% on Tradeweb and the thirty-year 4.5 basis points to around 5.70%, sterling was largely unmoved and the FTSE All-Share flat. The OBR put headroom at 15 billion pounds for 2029-30 against 24 billion forecast in March, at the low end of the pre-Budget cluster but inside it, with the fiscal rules kept; commentary settled on credible, uneventful, boring. This is the single biggest reason the pound goes from plus 1 to plus 2.

catalysts.event: Canada: Bank of Canada Overnight Rate, Rate Statement and Monetary Policy Report (red folder)
catalysts.note: Delivered. The overnight rate rose 25 basis points to 2.50%, in line with consensus and the first increase since July 2023, and TradingEconomics now carries the new rate. The Monetary Policy Report carried the content rather than the decision: 2027 inflation to 3.1% from the 2.0% projected in July and 2026 growth to 1.0% from 0.7%.

catalysts.event: Canada: Bank of Canada press conference with Governor Macklem (red folder)
catalysts.note: Held. Macklem framed the hike as insurance against energy pass-through - needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill into the rest of the economy - while refusing a sequence: no predetermined path, decisions one meeting at a time, further increases proceeding carefully. December 9 is about 42% priced, so this is optionality bought rather than a cycle started.

catalysts.event: United States: Federal Funds Rate decision and FOMC Statement (red folder)
catalysts.note: Delivered and verified on the primary source. The target range was held at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, with the statement approved by a 10-2 vote rather than September's 12-0: Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack preferred a quarter-point increase. Hammack dissented the same way in July; for Cook it is the first dissent in four years, which is where the information is. The statement says inflation remains elevated and that the Committee will deliver price stability, describes job gains as having kept pace with the workforce, and - against yesterday's read - does not mention energy prices at all.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC press conference with Chair Warsh (red folder)
catalysts.note: Held. Warsh gave no December signal, consistent with a Chair who has opposed forward guidance since August rather than with a dovish turn, and said politics played no role with the midterms six days away. The repricing that was not published when the commentary pass ran has now printed: CME FedWatch has December 9 at about 81.4% against 75.1% the previous morning, Polymarket at 82% from roughly 77%, and Bloomberg headlines bond traders at 90%. Oxford Economics reads the two hike dissents plus the statement wording as pointing to December.

catalysts.event: United States: Advance Q3 GDP q/q and September Core PCE Price Index m/m (BEA red folder)
catalysts.note: Released and verified on TradingEconomics. Advance Q3 GDP came in at 3.4% annualised against a 3.2% forecast, the fastest in a year, up from a Q2 that TE now carries at 2.2% - the 1.5% previous quoted on the calendar is the superseded vintage. September core PCE was 0.3% m/m, exactly in line, but August was revised up to 0.3% from 0.2%, so TE prints the previous at 0.3%; the annual core rate rose to 3.1% from 3.0% and headline PCE to 3.6% from 3.4%, both as expected. The one disinflationary detail sits inside the GDP report: Q3 core PCE prices slowed to 2.5% annualised from 3.3%. Initial claims printed 194K against a 199K consensus. DXY was 102.209 and plus 0.01% five minutes after the print - the beat this file said was already paid for, and it was.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB Main Refinancing Rate and Monetary Policy Statement (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released and verified against the ECB press release and TradingEconomics: all three key rates held, deposit facility 2.50%, main refinancing 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90%, exactly in line. The signal was the text, and it leaned against the December hike rather than towards it. The Governing Council repeated that it is not pre-committing to a particular rate path - the same formula as September - and added two observations September did not carry: that underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage, and that financing conditions have tightened since the last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth. The hawkish leg is energy: rising energy prices pose upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth, and the increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock is likely to drive up inflation and lower growth. APP and PEPP continue to run down with no reinvestment and the TPI remains available. EUR/USD went from 1.11440 and minus 0.09% before the decision to 1.11222 and minus 0.29% after it; Euro Stoxx Banks fell 0.82%. The preview below is kept for the record. A hold is near-unanimous: 70 of 73 economists in a Reuters poll expect the deposit rate to stay at 2.50% and the main refinancing rate at 2.65%, with OIS pricing about a 3% chance of a move. The content is therefore the signal rather than the decision - 64 of 73 expect 25 basis points in December and the market prices roughly 70 basis points of hikes over twelve months. September HICP at 3.8% is a three-year high, but every activity series has turned and FXStreet notes Governing Council communication since September has been less hawkish than Lagarde's own tone.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB President Lagarde announces she will step down on 7 February 2027
catalysts.note: Announced in an ECB press release at 11:00 CET, before the decision and after this morning’s report was built. Lagarde informed the Governing Council and European Council President Antonio Costa that she will leave on 7 February 2027, about nine months before her eight-year term ends; the release gives no reason and says the successor will be appointed by the European Council under Article 283 of the Treaty. Press reports name Pablo Hernandez de Cos and Klaas Knot among the frontrunners, which the ECB has not confirmed. The FX relevance is not the February date but the guidance horizon: on the ECB’s own published calendar a president leaving on 7 February chairs exactly two more decisions, 17 December and 4 February, which is one more reason the Council is unwilling to pre-commit to a path. FXStreet reported no visible euro impact on the announcement itself.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB press conference with President Lagarde (red folder)
catalysts.note: Held and read against the ECB’s own introductory statement plus wire coverage of the Q and A; the ECB has published the introductory statement but not yet the Q and A transcript, so the quotations below are from wire reporting rather than the official record. The press conference reversed its own statement, which is the tradeable fact. Lagarde said the decision to hold was taken unanimously but that the Governing Council debated whether a rate hike was appropriate; that the direction of travel is quite clear on rates; that the inter-meeting period of six weeks will give the Council a lot more information; and that there is no plan to restrict the number of meetings. On transmission she said that should market developments threaten it, the ECB has instruments to respond - notably cool on actually activating the Transmission Protection Instrument for France, whose ten-year is 4.910% near quarter-century highs with the OAT-Bund spread wider at about 158 basis points. The dovish half came from her too: indirect effects from the energy surge have increased, but there is no risk of second-round effects beyond what is in the projections, wage pressures remain moderate, compensation per employee grew 3.3% in Q2 from 3.6% in Q1, and the ECB wage tracker points to 2.5-2.8% for the remaining months of 2026 and an average 2.6% for the first three quarters of 2027. From the introductory statement, new detail the 13:15 release did not carry: September HICP 3.8% from 3.2% with energy inflation 18.9% from 14.3%, inflation excluding energy 2.3% from 2.1%, services 3.2% from 3.0%, goods 1.1% from 1.2%, food 1.3% from 1.1%; unemployment 6.4% in August; energy prices now above the September staff projection baseline, keeping headline well above target over the coming quarters; and financing conditions tightened, with corporate credit standards tightening in Q3 and mortgage demand declining substantially. Market verdict: EUR/USD made a fresh 17-month low at 1.1105 on the statement and recovered to 1.11503 and minus 0.03%, EUR/GBP 0.83533 is a 17-month high for sterling, the DAX closed the gap upward to 26,100.90 and plus 1.54% at a two-month high, EU50 plus 0.74%, Euro Stoxx Banks minus 0.82%, Bund 3.3334%. Not verifiable: any post-conference repricing of December in OIS or futures - no source published updated odds in time for this pass.

catalysts.note: The tradeable item of the week for the yen. Sources say the Bank may raise its inflation outlook for the next fiscal year because higher oil prices are exerting longer-than-expected price pressure, which would pre-commit a December hike without forcing a move now - the cleanest yen-positive outcome available. JPYBASKET is the single cleanest instrument for it and the opposite ticket to every XXX/JPY line in this file.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz: Iran-US negotiations and the insurance premium
catalysts.note: The single rolling variable in this file. Iran said on October 28 the strait could reopen in four to five days if the US lifts its blockade; the IMO said on October 27 that the route contains mines and it cannot guarantee safe transit, CENTCOM disputes the closure, and the UN is pushing for talks. War-risk cover runs 6-10% of hull value per transit against 0.15-0.25% pre-war, transits fell from 85 a day to four by October 18, and more than thirty VLCCs have been damaged with eleven hit in October. An accepted deal is the invalidation for USOIL, CAD and the whole haven complex at once.

geopolitics: The transmission chain is unchanged and the new thing in it is a diplomatic off-ramp rather than an escalation. Iran said on October 28 that the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within four to five days if the United States lifts its blockade, and that conditional offer is why WTI is 101.276 and minus 1.46%, Brent 114.031 and minus 1.12%, and the weekly gain has halved to plus 1.82% from the plus 4.40% this file quoted yesterday. Hold that against the physical facts, all of which postdate the escalation and none of which have changed: the IRGC declared the strait closed on October 26, the International Maritime Organization said on October 27 that the Hormuz traffic route contains mines and that it cannot guarantee safe transit, more than thirty very large crude carriers have been damaged with eleven hit in October alone on a Reuters review of IMO and MarineTraffic data, and war-risk cover is quoted at 6-10% of hull value per transit against 0.15-0.25% before the war. Transits fell from 85 a day to four by October 18, and the barrels that still move do so at night in a US-protected lane that Tehran regards as illegal, at high cost in time, money and crews. CENTCOM disputes the closure and says the main shipping routes remain clear; the UN is pushing both sides toward talks. That configuration is why this file keeps USOIL long but cuts the conviction to LOW-MED. The premium is priced off insurable risk rather than off volumes, so rerouting caps the upside without deflating it - but an offer to reopen, even one conditional on a concession the United States has not made, is the first credible path to removing it, and the flip is an accepted deal rather than another soft session. The FX read follows the same logic and it is unusually tidy today. Crude is the terms-of-trade leg under a plus 2 Canada, so the Bank of Canada's October 28 hike to 2.50% - explicitly insurance against energy pass-through, with its 2027 inflation forecast lifted to 3.1% from 2.0% - is the position that an accepted deal would undercut first, which is why USD/CAD short, CAD/JPY long and CAD/CHF long all share one invalidation. The franc is the mirror: the SNB judged on September 24 that its threat of franc sales was no longer needed because war-induced haven flows had ebbed, so every short-franc line in this file - AUD/CHF, GBP/CHF, CAD/CHF, long USD/CHF - is implicitly short a Hormuz re-escalation, and EUR/CHF at 0.92222 sits a little closer to the level the Bank previously threatened to defend. Japan is the most energy-import-levered economy here and the Bank of Japan may lift next fiscal year's inflation forecast at 02:31 UTC tomorrow precisely because higher oil is pressing longer than expected, which makes the Outlook Report a second-order Hormuz trade. Gold holds 4,000 with the haven leg two-sided for the same reason, and losing that handle remains the file's tell for whether this risk is being priced as manageable. Elsewhere, the French question is the European political risk that matters more than the headline suggests: the French ten-year is 4.910% near quarter-century highs and the OAT-Bund spread has widened to about 158 basis points from 155.9 this morning, Euro Stoxx Banks is minus 10.23% on the month even after Lagarde firmed the December hike from the podium, and she stayed cool on activating the Transmission Protection Instrument, saying only that the ECB has instruments to respond should market developments threaten transmission - which is why EU50 is scored apart from the DAX. The US midterms on November 3 and the New Zealand general election on November 7 are the two political dates inside the next ten days.
